screens.title: Performance Optimization — Compute & Storage
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on practical choices that control application speed and cost. You will learn how to match EC2 instance families to C P U, memory, storage, and network needs, and how different EBS volume types trade cost for IOPS and throughput. We will explain when to use ephemeral instance store, and when to prefer network-attached EBS for persistence. For object storage, you will learn simple S3 performance patterns like distributing objects across prefixes, using multipart upload for large files, and when Transfer Acceleration helps geographically distant users. Finally, we cover caching strategies with ElastiCache and CloudFront to reduce backend load and latency. Each topic includes concrete examples and a hands-on lab you can run to compare gp2 and gp3 input and output with fio and to practice multipart uploads with the AWS CLI. By the end you will know which choices improve responsiveness, which are ephemeral optimizations, and how to validate performance with measurements. Keep in mind that monitoring and iterative testing are the final authority: right-sizing uses metrics, not guesswork.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Why They Matter
screens.narratorSegment: This page explains why each objective matters in practice and shows a quick mental model. Right-sizing instances prevents both wasted spend and throttled performance: a memory-optimized database tuned on an underpowered C P U will still be slow, and a C P U-optimized instance with little memory can cause swapping. EBS choices shape IOPS and throughput guarantees; gp3 gives a reliable baseline with the ability to provision more IOPS separately, while io2 is for heavy, sustained transactional workloads. S3 optimizations affect how quickly your application can read and write objects at scale — prefixing avoids hot key bottlenecks when many requests target similar object paths, and multipart upload parallelizes large transfers. Caching moves hot data to faster layers: ElastiCache reduces database hits and CloudFront reduces geographic latency. You will also practice a hands-on benchmark so you can see differences instead of guessing. Remember: measurement and iteration trump intuition.

screens.title: EC2 Instance Families Overview
screens.narratorSegment: EC2 instance families group similar resource profiles so you can choose a virtual server that aligns with your workload. General purpose families, such as the M series and burstable T instances, balance C P U, memory, and networking and are often the sensible default for application servers and small databases. Compute-optimized instances, the C family, deliver higher C P U per dollar and are suited to batch processing, HPC, and compute-heavy web services. Memory-optimized families like R, X, and Z are tuned for large in-memory datasets and are common for high-performance databases and in-memory caches. Storage-optimized families such as I, D, and H provide large local storage and high sequential or random input and output for NoSQL databases, data warehousing, or distributed file systems. Accelerated computing instances like P and G attach accelerators to improve ML training or graphics workloads. A common misconception is to pick an instance family by name rather than by measured resource profile; instead, identify whether C P U, memory, or disk input and output is the limiting factor and choose accordingly. For a concrete example, a web app with variable C P U bursts can use a burstable T instance, while a heavy in-memory cache benefits from an R-family instance. The takeaway: categorize your workload profile, then pick the family that optimizes that primary resource.

keyIdea.title: Pick a family by bottleneck
keyIdea.text: Identify whether CPU, memory, or storage I/O is the limiting factor and select the instance family optimized for that resource.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › EC2 Instance Families
Families at a glance
General Purpose — M, T
Balanced CPU, memory, and networking. T are burstable for variable CPU.
Compute Optimized — C
Higher CPU density for compute-bound workloads.
Memory Optimized — R, X, Z
Large RAM for databases and in-memory analytics.
Storage Optimized — I, D, H
High I/O or throughput on local disks for big data.
Accelerated — P, G, F
Hardware accelerators for ML, graphics, or specialized compute.
Example & decision checklist
Example: a bursty web application with occasional high CPU peaks and otherwise light memory needs. A burstable T instance can lower cost, while a C-family instance might be chosen for sustained heavy CPU. Decision checklist:
  • Measure CPU, memory, network, and disk I/O over representative workloads.
  • Identify the dominant constraint (CPU, memory, or storage I/O).
  • Choose the family that optimizes that resource and test under load.
Common Mistake
Choosing a family by default name instead of by measured resource usage leads to poor performance or wasted cost.
Pro Tip
Use CloudWatch metrics to identify the resource bottleneck before resizing or changing families.
Key Takeaway

Match instance family to the primary workload bottleneck, then validate with monitored metrics.

screens.title: Right-sizing Instances with Monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: Right-sizing is a repeatable process: measure, analyze, decide, and validate. Start by collecting CloudWatch metrics over representative traffic: C P U utilization, memory usage, network packets, and disk input and output. Memory metrics sometimes require the CloudWatch agent. Next, analyze the metrics to identify the dominant constraint. Is C P U spiking and throttling? Are reads and writes queuing on disk? Is network bandwidth saturating? Use these answers to choose an instance family and size: a C P U bottleneck suggests compute-optimized instances, persistent high memory usage suggests memory-optimized instances, and heavy input and output suggests storage-optimized instances or faster EBS. Choose a candidate instance and run a load test or a staging deployment. Monitor the same metrics to verify the change improved the bottleneck without introducing new issues. If cost is a concern, consider burstable instances for intermittent loads, but test for steady-state performance. A common misconception is to scale vertically without exploring horizontal scaling or caching; sometimes adding a cache or splitting services removes the need for a larger instance. In practice, iterate: adjust size, re-measure, and pick the smallest instance that meets requirements under realistic load.

keyIdea.text: Use CloudWatch metrics to identify bottlenecks, pick the appropriate family, and validate improvements under load.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Right-sizing Process
Step-by-step
  1. Measure: Collect CPU, memory, network, and disk metrics over a representative period.
  2. Analyze: Identify which resource is the limiting factor and whether the pattern is steady or bursty.
  3. Decide: Pick an instance family and size that optimizes the bottleneck.
  4. Validate: Run load tests or staging validation and re-measure to confirm improvement.
  5. Iterate: Adjust or explore caching and horizontal scaling if vertical scaling is insufficient.
Example
An app with sustained 90% CPU and low memory should move from a general purpose M instance to a compute-optimized C instance and be retested under load.
Supporting tips
  • Use CloudWatch alarms to alert when metrics cross thresholds that indicate resizing is needed.
  • Remember that burstable instances are cost-effective for intermittent CPU spikes but unsuitable for sustained heavy CPU.
  • Consider caching or service decomposition before choosing a much larger instance.
Key Takeaway

Right-sizing requires measured data and iterative testing; do not guess based on peak moments alone.

screens.title: EBS Volume Types and Performance
screens.narratorSegment: EBS volume types map cost to performance characteristics such as IOPS and throughput. General Purpose SSD volumes, like gp3 and gp2, serve many transactional workloads. gp3 is the newer generation and provides a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB per second throughput at no extra cost, and it allows you to provision higher IOPS or throughput independently. gp2 ties burst performance to volume size, which can lead to unexpected limits for small volumes. Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes, io1 and io2, are designed for sustained high IOPS needs, for example, critical databases with heavy transaction rates; io2 provides higher durability and more IOPS per GiB than io1. For throughput-focused, sequential workloads, Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) is cost effective. Cold HDD (sc1) is the lowest cost option for infrequently accessed data. When selecting a volume, map your application's IOPS and throughput requirements to the volume's guarantees. A common mistake is using gp2 when gp3 provides a better baseline and flexible provisioning. Always test EBS performance with realistic workloads: theoretical specs are a guide, but measured IOPS and latency under load tell the real story.

keyIdea.title: Select volumes by IOPS & throughput needs
keyIdea.text: Map your workload's IOPS and throughput requirements to EBS types and validate with benchmarks.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › EBS Volume Types
Volume comparison
gp3
Baseline 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s throughput; IOPS/throughput provisionable independently.
gp2
Burst model tied to volume size; can be limited on small volumes.
io1 / io2
Provisioned IOPS for sustained high-performance transactional workloads; io2 adds durability and more IOPS per GiB.
st1 / sc1
HDD options for throughput-heavy or infrequent workloads; lower cost for large sequential reads/writes.
Practical guidance
  • For transactional databases with sustained IOPS, prefer io2 to ensure consistent latency.
  • For general-purpose servers, gp3 offers predictable baseline performance and the ability to provision extra IOPS if needed.
  • For log processing or data warehousing where throughput matters, consider st1 for cost-effective sequential throughput.
Common Mistake
Assuming gp2 is sufficient for high IOPS workloads; gp3 often provides a better baseline and cost control.
Key Takeaway

Choose volumes by the IOPS and throughput your application needs, and validate using real workload tests.

screens.title: gp3 vs gp2 vs io2 — Practical Differences
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing gp3, gp2, and io2 helps you select the right balance of cost and performance. gp3 provides a reliable baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB per second throughput and lets you provision additional IOPS and throughput separately, which is useful when you need predictable performance without increasing volume size. gp2 ties burst capacity to volume size so small volumes might not meet bursty production demands. io2 volumes are designed for sustained, high IOPS workloads like high-transaction databases; they allow you to provision the IOPS you expect consistently and offer higher durability. For example, a general-purpose web server often does well on gp3, while a primary database with sustained high transactions benefits from io2. A common misconception is to assume larger volume size always improves performance; with gp3 you decouple size from performance so you can keep storage smaller while provisioning required IOPS. Always test realistic workloads using tools like fio to observe actual IOPS and latency. The practical rule: use gp3 for most transactional needs, move to io2 when you need sustained, provisioned IOPS and greater durability, and avoid relying on gp2 burst behavior for steady production load.

keyIdea.title: Decouple size and performance
keyIdea.text: gp3 decouples volume size from baseline performance; io2 provides predictable, provisioned IOPS for heavy transactional workloads.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › gp3 vs gp2 vs io2
Side-by-side
gp3
Baseline 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s; provision IOPS and throughput independently.
gp2
Burst model tied to volume size; may not sustain high IOPS on small volumes.
io2
Provisioned IOPS and higher durability for high-transaction databases.
Example scenario
A transactional database requires low latency and 10,000 sustained IOPS. gp3 could be provisioned to reach that level, but many production databases instead choose io2 for its durability guarantees and predictable sustained IOPS characteristics. For a general application server with modest I/O, gp3 delivers reliable baseline performance at a lower cost when decoupling size and IOPS matters.
Check your assumptions
Do not assume volume size equals performance. Use benchmarking under realistic load to confirm IOPS and latency meet application needs.
Key Takeaway

Use gp3 for most transactional needs and io2 when you require sustained, provisioned IOPS and higher durability; always benchmark.

screens.title: Instance Store vs EBS — Ephemeral vs Persistent
screens.narratorSegment: Instance store and EBS serve different purposes and are chosen based on persistence and performance needs. Instance store is physically attached to the host machine and offers very high random input and output performance, making it a great fit for temporary data such as scratch space, caches, and intermediate computation where data loss on instance termination is acceptable. The critical limitation is ephemerality: if the instance stops, terminates, or fails, the data is lost. For persistent needs you should use EBS, which is network-attached and survives instance stop and restart. EBS also supports snapshots for backups. A practical example: a data analytics job that reads large datasets from S3 and writes temporary intermediate results might use instance store for that scratch space to gain throughput and reduce EBS costs, knowing the results are transient and can be re-created. A mistake is treating instance store like persistent storage. When durability matters for the primary dataset, choose EBS and consider io2 or gp3 depending on IOPS requirements. Always plan for failure domains: if your workload cannot tolerate data loss, use durable volumes and backups.

keyIdea.text: Use instance store for temporary, high-performance scratch data; use EBS for persistent storage and backups.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Instance Store vs EBS
Instance Store
Physically attached, very high random I/O, ephemeral. Good for caches, buffers, and scratch data that can be recomputed.
Use when
Temporary high-throughput scratch space where data loss on termination is acceptable.
EBS
Network-attached, persistent across stops, supports snapshots and different performance tiers like gp3 and io2.
Use when
Data must persist beyond instance lifetime or require snapshots, backups, or replication.
Example scenario
A distributed analytics job that downloads raw input from S3, processes it, and uploads final results can use instance store for intermediate scratch files to maximize I/O performance, since the raw data and final results are stored in durable S3. Do not use instance store for the system drive if you need persistence across stops.
Common Mistake
Treating instance store as persistent storage; losing data on termination is a risk if used incorrectly.
Pro Tip
Use instance store for temporary scratch and EBS for any data that needs snapshot or backup features.

screens.title: S3 Performance Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: S3 scales to high request rates, but best practices help you get consistent performance. For request-rate scaling, distribute keys across prefixes so that traffic does not create hot partitions. For example, instead of using a single predictable path for many objects, introduce functional or time-based prefixes that spread requests. For large object uploads, use multipart upload: breaking the object into parts and uploading them concurrently reduces wall-clock time and makes retries easier for individual parts. The AWS CLI uses multipart upload automatically for sufficiently large files, but the pattern is the same: create parts, upload parts in parallel, then complete the multipart upload. For geographically distant users, S3 Transfer Acceleration routes data over optimized network paths via edge locations to the S3 region, which can reduce latency and improve throughput. However, Transfer Acceleration is most useful when clients are far from the bucket region; measure first to ensure it helps your scenario. Always test with realistic traffic patterns and sizes; a common misconception is that S3 performance tuning is only about object size, but naming patterns and client network paths matter as much as object size.

keyIdea.title: Spread requests and parallelize uploads
keyIdea.text: Use prefixes to avoid hot keys, multipart uploads for large objects, and measure transfer acceleration benefits for remote users.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › S3 Best Practices
Prefixing for scale
Distribute object keys across prefixes to avoid hot partitions. For example, organize objects by date or logical shard so requests are spread across internal partitions.
Multipart Upload
Split large objects into parts, upload parts in parallel, then complete the upload to speed transfers and simplify retries of individual parts.
Transfer Acceleration
Routes uploads through edge locations for clients far from the bucket region. Measure to confirm benefit and cost trade-offs before enabling.
Example Key Layout
Use s3://mybucket/2023-01/01/log.txt instead of putting every file under a single logs/ prefix to spread request load.
Key Takeaway

S3 performance depends on key design, parallel uploads, and client network paths. Test with realistic patterns.

screens.title: Multipart Uploads and AWS CLI
screens.narratorSegment: Multipart upload divides a large object into parts that are uploaded in parallel and recombined by the storage service. This reduces overall wall-clock time for large files and makes retries smaller and faster because individual parts can be re-sent. The AWS CLI will automatically use multipart upload for large files, but it's helpful to understand the flow: initiate a multipart upload, upload parts with part numbers, and then complete the upload. Practically, you can create a large dummy file and use the AWS CLI to transfer it; the client will manage multipart parts under the hood, enabling concurrency. For a concrete lab, generate a 600 megabyte file and run aws s3 cp to a bucket; the transfer will use multipart upload and you can observe throughput. A common misconception is that multipart upload is only for fault tolerance — it is primarily a performance tool for parallelizing uploads and making retries efficient. After the upload, validate the object in the bucket and teardown resources. Understanding multipart upload helps you reason about transfer time and when to use tools like Transfer Acceleration for clients spread across long distances.

For a concrete lab, generate a 600 megabyte file and run aws s3 cp to a bucket; the transfer will use multipart upload and you can observe throughput. A common misconception is that multipart upload is only for fault tolerance — it is primarily a performance tool for parallelizing uploads and making retries efficient. After the upload, validate the object in the bucket and teardown resources. Understanding multipart upload helps you reason about transfer time and when to use tools like Transfer Acceleration for clients spread across long distances.

keyIdea.title: Parallelize large transfers
keyIdea.text: Multipart upload breaks files into parts so uploads run in parallel and retries only resend failed parts.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Multipart Upload
Concept
Multipart upload splits a large object into parts, uploads them concurrently, then completes the upload. This reduces time and localizes retries to failed parts.
When to use
Large objects (hundreds of megabytes and above) or when parallel upload increases throughput.
CLI example
Create a large file and use the AWS CLI; the client manages multipart upload automatically for large objects.
# generate a 600MB file on Linux
dd if=/dev/urandom of=largefile.bin bs=1M count=600

# upload with the AWS CLI (uses multipart for large files)
aws s3 cp largefile.bin s3://YOUR_BUCKET_NAME/largefile.bin --expected-size 629145600
Note: the CLI automates multipart parts and completion; monitor transfer speed to compare performance.
Key Takeaway

Multipart upload parallelizes large file transfers and simplifies retries by allowing individual part re-uploads.

screens.title: Caching Strategies — ElastiCache Redis vs Memcached
screens.narratorSegment: Caching can dramatically reduce latency and backend load when designed correctly. Amazon ElastiCache offers managed Redis and Memcached. Redis provides richer data structures, persistence options, and pub/sub capabilities, which make it suitable for session storage with occasional persistence, leaderboards, counters, and real-time features. Memcached is a simpler in-memory key-value cache that's easy to scale horizontally and is suitable for straightforward object caching. When deciding between them, consider whether you need advanced data structures or persistence: choose Redis for richer functionality and Memcached for light-weight object caches. Caching patterns include write-through, write-around, and cache-aside. Cache-aside, where application logic checks the cache first and falls back to the source if a miss occurs, is common in practice and is compatible with both Redis and Memcached. TTL selection matters; set time-to-live values based on how stale data can be without causing correctness issues. A common misconception is that caching always improves performance — misconfigured caches with very short TTLs or poor invalidation can add complexity and not reduce load. The practical rule is to cache hot, read-heavy data and design invalidation to maintain correctness.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › ElastiCache: Redis vs Memcached
Redis
Rich data structures, optional persistence, pub/sub. Good for sessions, leaderboards, and complex caching patterns.
When to choose
When you need sorted sets, pub/sub, or persistence options alongside caching.
Memcached
Simple in-memory key-value cache, easy to scale horizontally, ideal for basic object caching.
When to choose
When you only need straightforward caching and horizontal scaling with no persistence.
Caching pattern: Cache-aside
Applications check the cache first and fetch from the source on a miss, then populate the cache. TTL and invalidation strategies are crucial to avoid stale data.
Common Mistake
Setting TTLs too short or failing to design invalidation leads to cache churn and little benefit.
Pro Tip
Cache hot, read-heavy objects and monitor cache hit ratio to decide TTLs and sizing.
Key Takeaway

Choose Redis for richer functionality and Memcached for simple, scalable object caching; always design TTLs and invalidation around correctness.

screens.title: CloudFront Caching and Invalidation
screens.narratorSegment: CloudFront is a CDN that caches content at edge locations to reduce latency for global users. For static assets and cacheable A P I responses, serving from CloudFront brings data closer to users and reduces load on your origin. CloudFront can also accelerate dynamic content by optimizing network paths. When using CloudFront, design caching policies and TTLs according to how fresh content must be. Short TTLs increase origin requests and reduce cache benefits; long TTLs risk serving stale content. For changes that must be seen immediately, use invalidation requests to remove objects from the edge caches, but note that excessive invalidations are operationally costly. A practical strategy is to include versioned object names for assets that change frequently — update the object name so CloudFront treats it as a new entry without invalidation. A common misconception is relying solely on TTLs for immediate updates; versioning object names is usually more predictable at scale. Measure cache hit ratios and origin request counts to tune TTLs and invalidation behavior for best performance and cost balance. CloudFront Caching and Invalidation means use cloudfront to serve content from edge locations and use versioned object names rather than frequent invalidation for predictable freshness.. In practical terms, reducing global latency and maintaining freshness. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › CloudFront Caching
Why CloudFront
CloudFront caches content at edge locations around the world to reduce latency and origin load. It also offers features to accelerate dynamic content.
Cache Strategies
Set TTLs based on acceptable staleness, measure hit ratios, and use versioned object names to avoid frequent invalidations.
Operational advice
  • Monitor cache hit ratio and origin request count to understand performance impact.
  • Use versioned keys for assets that change often to avoid mass invalidations.
  • Reserve invalidation for emergency or infrequent updates; it can be slow and costly at scale.
Key Takeaway

CloudFront reduces global latency. Use versioned keys for frequent updates and reserve invalidation for exceptions.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity — Compare gp2 and gp3 with fio
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through comparing gp2 and gp3 performance using fio. Start by launching two similar EC2 instances in the same availability zone with Amazon Linux 2 and SSH access: one instance with a gp2 root volume and another with a gp3 root volume. Install fio on both machines using the package manager. Then run the same fio random write benchmark on each device to measure IOPS and throughput. Compare the results between the gp2 instance and the gp3 instance: gp3 should show a stronger baseline for IOPS and throughput at the same instance size. Remember to run tests at times that reflect real workload patterns, and tear down resources after the lab to avoid charges. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Hands-on: fio Benchmark
Lab steps summary
  1. Launch two t2.medium instances in the same AZ; one with gp2 root volume, one with gp3.
  2. Install fio: update packages and install the tool.
  3. Run identical fio benchmarks on each instance and compare IOPS/throughput.
  4. Analyze results and tear down resources when done.
Benchmark command
sudo yum update -y
sudo yum install -y fio
sudo fio --filename=/dev/xvda --direct=1 --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --numjobs=1 --size=1G --name=randwrite_test --iodepth=16 --group_reporting
Run the same command on both instances and record the reported IOPS and throughput, then compare.
Key Takeaway

Benchmarks reveal real performance differences; use them to choose the appropriate EBS type for production workloads.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the essential ideas to carry forward. First, pick EC2 instance families by the primary resource bottleneck — C P U, memory, or storage input and output — and validate with monitoring. Second, choose EBS volumes based on IOPS and throughput needs: gp3 offers a reliable baseline with provisionable IOPS, while io2 is for sustained high IOPS and higher durability. Third, instance store is high-performance but ephemeral and should be used only for temporary scratch data. Fourth, S3 performance depends on key design and parallel uploads; distribute keys across prefixes and use multipart uploads for large files. Fifth, caching with ElastiCache and CloudFront reduces backend load and latency, but cache freshness and invalidation must be planned. Finally, measurement and iteration are the final authority: benchmark and monitor to confirm optimizations actually improve the user experience. These concepts together let you balance cost, durability, and performance for real workloads.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Final Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: Use this checklist as a quick reminder when designing for performance. First, identify the dominant resource constraint and choose the instance family that optimizes that resource. Second, map application IOPS and throughput needs to EBS types; prefer gp3 for baseline performance and io2 for provisioned, durable IOPS. Third, use instance store only for temporary scratch data; do not rely on it for persistent datasets. Fourth, design S3 keys to spread request load, use multipart uploads for large objects, and consider Transfer Acceleration only after measuring benefit. Fifth, cache hot reads with ElastiCache and serve global content through CloudFront while designing sensible TTLs or using versioned keys to manage freshness. Finally, always validate your design with benchmarks such as fio and monitoring metrics to ensure the performance improvements are real and cost-effective. Keep this checklist handy as you iterate on your architecture.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on practical choices that control application speed and cost. You will learn how to match EC2 instance families to C P U, memory, storage, and network needs, and how different EBS volume types trade cost for IOPS and throughput. We will explain when to use ephemeral instance store, and when to prefer network-attached EBS for persistence. For object storage, you will learn simple S3 performance patterns like distributing objects across prefixes, using multipart upload for large files, and when Transfer Acceleration helps geographically distant users. Finally, we cover caching strategies with ElastiCache and CloudFront to reduce backend load and latency. Each topic includes concrete examples and a hands-on lab you can run to compare gp2 and gp3 input and output with fio and to practice multipart uploads with the AWS CLI. By the end you will know which choices improve responsiveness, which are ephemeral optimizations, and how to validate performance with measurements. Keep in mind that monitoring and iterative testing are the final authority: right-sizing uses metrics, not guesswork.

These objectives focus on measurable skills you should gain. First, you will be able to select EC2 instance types that match application workload needs — balancing C P U, memory, network, and storage input and output so you avoid overpaying or under-provisioning. Second, you will differentiate EBS volume types by their IOPS and throughput profiles so you can pick gp3, io2, st1, or sc1 for transactional, throughput, or archival use cases. Third, you will apply S3 performance best practices such as prefixing object keys, using multipart uploads for large objects, and knowing when Transfer Acceleration helps geographically distributed users. Fourth, you will design caching strategies using ElastiCache and CloudFront to reduce backend load and improve user response times. Each objective pairs a practical action with a reason why it matters: from lower latency to cost control and measurable user experience gains. By the end you'll also be prepared to validate choices through simple benchmarks and monitoring.

This page explains why each objective matters in practice and shows a quick mental model. Right-sizing instances prevents both wasted spend and throttled performance: a memory-optimized database tuned on an underpowered C P U will still be slow, and a C P U-optimized instance with little memory can cause swapping. EBS choices shape IOPS and throughput guarantees; gp3 gives a reliable baseline with the ability to provision more IOPS separately, while io2 is for heavy, sustained transactional workloads. S3 optimizations affect how quickly your application can read and write objects at scale — prefixing avoids hot key bottlenecks when many requests target similar object paths, and multipart upload parallelizes large transfers. Caching moves hot data to faster layers: ElastiCache reduces database hits and CloudFront reduces geographic latency. You will also practice a hands-on benchmark so you can see differences instead of guessing. Remember: measurement and iteration trump intuition.

EC2 instance families group similar resource profiles so you can choose a virtual server that aligns with your workload. General purpose families, such as the M series and burstable T instances, balance C P U, memory, and networking and are often the sensible default for application servers and small databases. Compute-optimized instances, the C family, deliver higher C P U per dollar and are suited to batch processing, HPC, and compute-heavy web services. Memory-optimized families like R, X, and Z are tuned for large in-memory datasets and are common for high-performance databases and in-memory caches. Storage-optimized families such as I, D, and H provide large local storage and high sequential or random input and output for NoSQL databases, data warehousing, or distributed file systems. Accelerated computing instances like P and G attach accelerators to improve ML training or graphics workloads. A common misconception is to pick an instance family by name rather than by measured resource profile; instead, identify whether C P U, memory, or disk input and output is the limiting factor and choose accordingly. For a concrete example, a web app with variable C P U bursts can use a burstable T instance, while a heavy in-memory cache benefits from an R-family instance. The takeaway: categorize your workload profile, then pick the family that optimizes that primary resource.

Right-sizing is a repeatable process: measure, analyze, decide, and validate. Start by collecting CloudWatch metrics over representative traffic: C P U utilization, memory usage, network packets, and disk input and output. Memory metrics sometimes require the CloudWatch agent. Next, analyze the metrics to identify the dominant constraint. Is C P U spiking and throttling? Are reads and writes queuing on disk? Is network bandwidth saturating? Use these answers to choose an instance family and size: a C P U bottleneck suggests compute-optimized instances, persistent high memory usage suggests memory-optimized instances, and heavy input and output suggests storage-optimized instances or faster EBS. Choose a candidate instance and run a load test or a staging deployment. Monitor the same metrics to verify the change improved the bottleneck without introducing new issues. If cost is a concern, consider burstable instances for intermittent loads, but test for steady-state performance. A common misconception is to scale vertically without exploring horizontal scaling or caching; sometimes adding a cache or splitting services removes the need for a larger instance. In practice, iterate: adjust size, re-measure, and pick the smallest instance that meets requirements under realistic load.

EBS volume types map cost to performance characteristics such as IOPS and throughput. General Purpose SSD volumes, like gp3 and gp2, serve many transactional workloads. gp3 is the newer generation and provides a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB per second throughput at no extra cost, and it allows you to provision higher IOPS or throughput independently. gp2 ties burst performance to volume size, which can lead to unexpected limits for small volumes. Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes, io1 and io2, are designed for sustained high IOPS needs, for example, critical databases with heavy transaction rates; io2 provides higher durability and more IOPS per GiB than io1. For throughput-focused, sequential workloads, Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) is cost effective. Cold HDD (sc1) is the lowest cost option for infrequently accessed data. When selecting a volume, map your application's IOPS and throughput requirements to the volume's guarantees. A common mistake is using gp2 when gp3 provides a better baseline and flexible provisioning. Always test EBS performance with realistic workloads: theoretical specs are a guide, but measured IOPS and latency under load tell the real story.

Comparing gp3, gp2, and io2 helps you select the right balance of cost and performance. gp3 provides a reliable baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB per second throughput and lets you provision additional IOPS and throughput separately, which is useful when you need predictable performance without increasing volume size. gp2 ties burst capacity to volume size so small volumes might not meet bursty production demands. io2 volumes are designed for sustained, high IOPS workloads like high-transaction databases; they allow you to provision the IOPS you expect consistently and offer higher durability. For example, a general-purpose web server often does well on gp3, while a primary database with sustained high transactions benefits from io2. A common misconception is to assume larger volume size always improves performance; with gp3 you decouple size from performance so you can keep storage smaller while provisioning required IOPS. Always test realistic workloads using tools like fio to observe actual IOPS and latency. The practical rule: use gp3 for most transactional needs, move to io2 when you need sustained, provisioned IOPS and greater durability, and avoid relying on gp2 burst behavior for steady production load.

Instance store and EBS serve different purposes and are chosen based on persistence and performance needs. Instance store is physically attached to the host machine and offers very high random input and output performance, making it a great fit for temporary data such as scratch space, caches, and intermediate computation where data loss on instance termination is acceptable. The critical limitation is ephemerality: if the instance stops, terminates, or fails, the data is lost. For persistent needs you should use EBS, which is network-attached and survives instance stop and restart. EBS also supports snapshots for backups. A practical example: a data analytics job that reads large datasets from S3 and writes temporary intermediate results might use instance store for that scratch space to gain throughput and reduce EBS costs, knowing the results are transient and can be re-created. A mistake is treating instance store like persistent storage. When durability matters for the primary dataset, choose EBS and consider io2 or gp3 depending on IOPS requirements. Always plan for failure domains: if your workload cannot tolerate data loss, use durable volumes and backups.

Here are the essential ideas to carry forward. First, pick EC2 instance families by the primary resource bottleneck — C P U, memory, or storage input and output — and validate with monitoring. Second, choose EBS volumes based on IOPS and throughput needs: gp3 offers a reliable baseline with provisionable IOPS, while io2 is for sustained high IOPS and higher durability. Third, instance store is high-performance but ephemeral and should be used only for temporary scratch data. Fourth, S3 performance depends on key design and parallel uploads; distribute keys across prefixes and use multipart uploads for large files. Use this checklist as a quick reminder when designing for performance. First, identify the dominant resource constraint and choose the instance family that optimizes that resource. Second, map application IOPS and throughput needs to EBS types; prefer gp3 for baseline performance and io2 for provisioned, durable IOPS. Third, use instance store only for temporary scratch data; do not rely on it for persistent datasets. Fourth, design S3 keys to spread request load, use multipart uploads for large objects, and consider Transfer Acceleration only after measuring benefit. Fifth, cache hot reads with ElastiCache and serve global content through CloudFront while designing sensible TTLs or using versioned keys to manage freshness. Finally, always validate your design with benchmarks such as fio and monitoring metrics to ensure the performance improvements are real and cost-effective.
